title: Epic: RBAC v2 + permission inventory (control plane + console + private)
creator: Marcus Lin
description:
Context
We currently have a mix of coarse RBAC v1 gates + service-specific checks across the control plane, console backend, and admin/support tooling. This is becoming a blocker for enterprise security reviews (custom roles, least privilege, separation of duties, auditability), and it increases the chance of inconsistent enforcement as new endpoints are added.

This epic is the project container for moving Redwood Inference to RBAC v2: a consistent, fine-grained authorization model with an explicit permission inventory, shared check library, policy bundle/versioning, audit-log enrichment for authz decisions, and a safe migration plan (dual-eval + feature flags).

Goals
- Produce a complete inventory of sensitive actions across:
  - Control plane APIs (org/project/workspace admin, keys, rollouts, billing, SSO)
  - Console backend endpoints + UI actions that hit those endpoints
  - Dedicated operational tooling (capacity, autoscaling/pool config)
  - Private deployment admin flows (installer/admin endpoints, offline update flows)
  - Support/break-glass operations (impersonation, elevated session)
- Define RBAC v2 primitives and naming:
  - Resource / Action / Scope taxonomy
  - Default roles and separation of duties (Org Admin, Billing Admin, Security Admin, Developer, Read-only, Support/Impersonation)
  - Policy bundle schema + versioning
- Implement a unified permission-check path used consistently across services (gateway and/or service middleware) with:
  - standardized 403 reason codes
  - structured logging for decisions
  - strong unit + integration test coverage
- Deliver safe migration from RBAC v1 -> RBAC v2:
  - dual-evaluation (shadow) mode with metrics
  - staged enforcement by tier (Hosted -> Dedicated -> Private)
  - rollback plan and customer comms checklist
- Establish governance so new endpoints cannot ship without declaring permissions + wiring checks (CI conformance).

Non-goals (initial scope)
- Data-plane (token-level inference) authorization beyond tenant/project scoping.
- Deep refactors to IdP/SSO integrations except where needed to map group/claims -> role assignments.
- Re-architecting the entire console UI; focus is role management + gating sensitive flows.

Key stakeholders
- Security Eng: Marcus Lin (exec owner), Kevin Osei (audit logging), Hanae Suzuki (Private secure defaults)
- Platform/Control Plane: Ethan Park (lead), Kaitlyn Nguyen (authz implementation lead), Jordan Lee (policy engine)
- Console: Chloe Martin (backend lead), Jada Williams (console architecture)
- SRE: Sean Gallagher (break-glass workflows), Rafael Mendes (incident-time access)
- Product: Naomi Feldman (RBAC product owner), Marissa Cole (Console PM), Vivek Kulkarni (Private PM)

Milestones (target 8–12 weeks)
M1 — Permission inventory complete (2–3 weeks)
- Inventory sheet populated for control plane + console endpoints.
- Sensitivity rubric applied (P0/P1/P2) with owners.
- Gaps captured: missing/partial checks, legacy gates, unclear ownership.

M2 — RBAC v2 model & policy format locked (2–3 weeks)
- Resource/action taxonomy documented + naming conventions agreed.
- Default role matrix reviewed by Security + PM + Solutions Eng.
- ADR merged for policy evaluation semantics + versioning approach.

M3 — Shared library + core integrations (3–5 weeks)
- Authz library implemented with caching + metrics.
- Gateway/service enforcement standard implemented in control plane.
- Console backend routes updated to enforce RBAC v2.

M4 — Audit logging + explainability (1–2 weeks, overlaps)
- Authz decision context in audit logs (allow/deny, policy version, role IDs, reason codes).
- Exporter compatibility verified for SIEM.

M5 — Migration & rollout (2–4 weeks)
- Dual-eval (v1 + v2) shipping, shadow-deny dashboards available.
- Enforced rollout by tier with feature flags.
- Deprecation plan and comms for Dedicated/Private.

M6 — Governance (ongoing)
- CI conformance: endpoints must declare required permission and wire an authz check.
- Review checklist for adding new sensitive actions + evidence artifacts for SOC2/ISO.

Acceptance criteria (epic-level)
- A single, documented permission inventory exists and is maintained.
- All in-scope sensitive actions have a corresponding RBAC v2 permission and are enforced consistently.
- Every authorization decision is attributable and explainable in logs (actor, roles, policy version, allow/deny, reason).
- Migration runs in shadow mode with measurable, triaged deltas before enforcement.
- Break-glass/support flows are time-bounded and auditable.

Implementation notes / decisions in progress
- Evaluation semantics: leaning toward deny-overrides for explicit denies + allow rules for roles; confirm via ADR.
- Caching: per-org policy/role assignment cache with explicit invalidation on role changes; metrics required (hit rate + eval latency).
- Enforcement placement: gateway should do coarse authn + basic tenant scoping; services remain source of truth for fine-grained authz checks (avoid bypass paths).

Risks / open questions
- Performance overhead on hot paths (must remain low-latency). Need microbench + caching strategy.
- Backwards compatibility: avoid accidental privilege loss for enterprise admins and internal support workflows.
- Policy distribution for Private / air-gapped: version skew handling and signed bundle update mechanism.
- Role UX: enterprise wants custom roles; phased approach vs GA requirement.

Links (working set)
- Confluence: RBAC v2 overview / role definitions / migration plan (see Security & Compliance space)
- Policy bundle repo: initial v0.1 policy bundle PRs
- GitHub: control plane middleware + error reason codes + cache/invalidation + dual-eval
- Dashboards: shadow-deny metrics + authz evaluation latency

Work breakdown
See sub-issues for inventory crawler, taxonomy, shared authz lib, integrations (control plane + console), audit logging, private policy distribution, migration, and threat modeling.
comments: 2025-01-23 (Marcus Lin): Marking this P0 given HelixBank and Apex Cyber separation-of-duties requirements. We need a concrete role matrix + auditability story in the next security review cycle. Assigning Ethan as DRI for engineering execution; Naomi to coordinate PM/design dependencies.

2025-01-28 (Ethan Park): Kicked off inventory. Control plane endpoints: org/project admin, API keys, model rollouts, billing, SSO config. Console backend audit in progress with Chloe. Creating ENG-5382 for a crawler to seed route list so we don’t miss anything.

2025-02-03 (Kaitlyn Nguyen): Proposed resource/action naming: org.*, project.*, billing.*, security.*, dedicated.*, private.*. Need a hard rule: actions reflect intent (create_key, rotate_key) not HTTP verbs. Drafting ENG-5383.

2025-02-10 (Jordan Lee): Policy engine prototype supports policy bundles with semver + schema validation. Question remains: do we allow explicit denies for exception handling (e.g., block audit export) or keep allow-only for simplicity. Will capture in ADR and review with Security + SRE for break-glass semantics.

2025-02-17 (Kevin Osei): Audit logging requirements: must log decision + reason codes on deny and on high-risk allow (P0). Include policy_version, role_ids, and actor_type (user/service/support). I’ll drive ENG-5387 and align exporter compatibility.

2025-02-24 (Sean Gallagher): On-call needs time-bounded elevated sessions with explicit approval + alerting. Current ad-hoc admin toggles aren’t acceptable for audits. Please ensure break-glass design doesn’t block incident mitigation actions (e.g., suspend runaway org, rotate compromised key) but requires additional controls + post-incident review.

2025-03-04 (Connor O'Brien): Migration plan: dual-eval with shadow-deny metrics for 2 weeks in Hosted, then staged enforcement. Dedicated goes next (autoscaling/pool config gating has customer risk). Private needs bundle distribution story + upgrade path before enforcement. Targeting enforcement canary end of March if shadow deltas stabilize.
